Hook: Around 1969 the economist Thomas Schelling began a game with coins on a checkerboard. Two kinds of coin, scattered at random, with a tenth of the squares left empty. Each coin looks at its eight neighbours. The rule: a coin is content if at least a third of its neighbours are its own kind. Otherwise it moves to an empty square where it would be content. No coin minds being in the minority, and no coin wants a neighbourhood of its own kind. Here is the board, played round by round.

In the first round 239 coins are discontented, and move. Each move makes some neighbours less content, and they move in turn. After 7 rounds nobody wants to move, and the average coin's neighbours are 76 percent its own kind, up from half. Mild preferences, an extreme result: a pattern that nobody chose. Schelling published the model in 1971, and it became a classic of how choices about where to live add up to a map.

People sort themselves at every scale, and so does economic activity. Here are America's ten largest metropolitan areas in 2024. The country's 387 metropolitan areas hold 294 million people; the ten largest hold 30 percent of them, and New York alone 19.9 million, more than most countries. Land is cheap almost everywhere, yet people pay enormous rents to crowd into a few places.

This part's question: why is economic activity piled up in a few places, and what does that do to the people in them? Why do people and firms crowd together, and pay so much to do it? Why are the sizes of cities so regular, and their rents so high? What does a place do to the children who grow up in it? And can policy move economic activity, and should it?
Economics, Built. Part thirty-seven: cities and regions.

Here is the plan. Schelling's board, played; the rings of land use around a market town; and the model of a city with one centre. Why cities exist at all, the strange regularity of their sizes, and how a country splits into a core and a periphery. Spatial equilibrium, where wages, rents and the pleasures of a place move together; the supply of housing; and rent control. What neighbourhoods do to children; the Berlin Wall as an experiment; railways and highways. And policies aimed at places, two dials, and the frontier: working from home, and the climate.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: Schelling's rule.

Your turn. Every coin is content as long as a third of its neighbours are its own kind. At the start the average coin's neighbours are 50 percent its own kind. When the board settles, what will that share be? About half, because such tolerant coins hardly need to move; about sixty percent; about three quarters; or over ninety percent. Pause, and choose.

The answer is C. The share climbs from 50 percent to 76 in 7 rounds, and the board ends in large blocks of one kind. Coins content with half their neighbours alike end at 86 percent. Each move by one discontented coin leaves its old neighbours a little less content, and the movements cascade.

Now play it for every tolerance. Each point is the share of like neighbours when the board stops, against the share each coin wants. The curve rises far above the line of what anyone asked for: coins wanting a quarter alike end with well over half, coins wanting a half end near ninety percent. Past about two thirds the board never settles: someone is always discontented, and the churn keeps it mixed. The model shows that mild preferences can produce stark segregation. It does not show that real segregation comes from mild preferences: prices, laws, lending and discrimination sort people too, and Part thirty-nine returns to them. Credit where it is due: the sociologist James Sakoda had a similar checkerboard model in his dissertation of 1949.
Mono: In the 1960s William Alonso, Edwin Mills and Richard Muth turned von Thünen's farmers into commuters. A town of a million households, each earning sixty thousand dollars, all working in one centre. Commuting costs about a thousand dollars a year for each kilometre from the centre. In equilibrium nobody can gain by moving, so every location must be equally good. Move one kilometre out and your commute costs more; the rent on your floor space must fall by exactly as much. That condition is a differential equation for the rent gradient, and here is its solution: rent falls about 6.7 percent a kilometre near the centre. The town ends at 19 kilometres, where housing can no longer outbid farming for land.

Developers build up where land is dear. Here is the town from the side, each bar the floor space built on a square metre of land: towers at the centre, houses at the edge. Now give everyone a car, halving the cost of commuting. The rent gradient flattens, and the town spreads out: its edge moves from 19 kilometres to 31, the density at the centre falls by 74 percent, and the share of households within eight kilometres from 69 percent to 33. Instead, give everyone the lift and steel frames, making height forty percent cheaper to build. The town grows up, not out: the same edge and the same densities, but taller buildings, and 224 square metres for each household at the centre instead of 153. The car helped make the American suburb, and the lift helped make Manhattan; both come out of this one equation.
Agglo: Why pay those rents? Alfred Marshall wrote in 1890 that where a trade gathers, its mysteries become no mysteries, but are as it were in the air. Gilles Duranton and Diego Puga sorted the reasons into three. Sharing: a big city supports one large airport, specialised suppliers and lawyers that many firms use. Matching: in a thick labour market workers find jobs that suit them, and firms find workers, better and faster. Learning: ideas spread face to face, and young workers learn by watching the best. Against them stand the rents, the commutes and the congestion of the last chapter. A city is as large as the balance allows.

How much more productive does density make a worker? The number economists want is the agglomeration elasticity. On the Island I planted it: doubling a town's density raises everyone's productivity by about 2 percent, an elasticity of 0.03. Each dot is one of sixty towns. Fit a line across towns and you find 0.057, nearly double the truth. The planted line is flatter. The trouble is sorting: abler workers choose denser towns, so dense towns pay more partly because of who lives there. Cities attract talent, and talent is not the same thing as productivity that a city creates.

The cure is to follow the same people as they move. A worker who moves from a sparse town to a dense one keeps their ability, so the change in their wage measures what the town did. On the Island the movers give 0.029, close to the planted 0.03. Pierre-Philippe Combes, Gilles Duranton, Laurent Gobillon and Sébastien Roux did this with French wage records. The raw elasticity was about 0.05; following workers brought it to 0.033; their preferred estimate, 0.02. Real, but modest: doubling density raises wages by one or two percent. The rest of the big-city premium is who lives there.
Zipf: In 1949 the linguist George Kingsley Zipf noticed a regularity in city sizes. Rank a country's cities by population and plot rank against size on logarithmic scales. The points fall near a straight line with a slope of about minus one: the second city is about half the size of the first, the tenth about a tenth. Rank times size is roughly constant. For America's largest hundred metropolitan areas in 2024 the exponent is 1.18, give or take 0.17; across all 387 it is 0.90. Not exact: Los Angeles is more than half New York's size. But a law this regular across countries and centuries asks for an explanation.

Here is one, from Xavier Gabaix in 1999. Suppose every town grows each year at a random rate whose distribution does not depend on the town's size: Robert Gibrat's law of proportional growth. Four towns' paths wander up and down. Add one more rule: no town can shrink below a floor, a small fraction of the average. Run twenty thousand towns for long enough and their sizes settle into a power law with an exponent of one over one minus the floor, here 1.05; the simulation gives 0.95. Zipf's law needs no planner and no special theory of cities: only growth that is random and proportional.

That makes Zipf's law one of the series' facts. In America's data the exponent is close to one. The theory: random, proportional growth with a floor. And Agora reproduces it. The fit is rougher at the very top, where a handful of giant cities sit, and it holds better for the large cities than for the small.
CorePeriphery: In 1991 Paul Krugman put Part thirty-six's variety and scale into geography. Two regions; farmers who stay put, half in each; and manufacturing workers who can move. Suppose a few more workers live in the north. They spend there, so the north is a bigger market; firms with economies of scale prefer to produce near the bigger market and ship to the smaller; with more firms in the north, more varieties are cheap there, so real wages are higher, and more workers come. The loop feeds itself. Against it: the farmers in the south still buy manufactures, and shipping to them is costly. Which force wins depends on the cost of transport.

Agora solves the model for every split of manufacturing between the regions, with manufactures forty percent of spending. The curve is the real wage in the north minus that in the south. When shipping costs are high, a hundred and ten percent of the good's value, the curve slopes down: a worker who moves north lowers the north's real wage relative to the south's, and has reason to go back. The even spread is stable. At seventy percent, the curve wiggles: the even spread is stable, but so is a core in either region. At fifty percent, the curve slopes up: anyone who moves north raises the gain from moving north, and everything ends up in one place.

Put every transport cost on one picture, and the equilibria make the shape geographers call the tomahawk. Solid lines are stable, dashed unstable. Start at the right, with shipping dear: industry is spread evenly, and nothing much changes as costs fall. Then, at 1.63, the even spread breaks, suddenly and completely: the economy tips into a core and a periphery. And the core, once formed, survives even if costs rise again, up to 1.81. Between the two points, history decides. Gradual change can have sudden effects, and a small advantage, like the north's few extra workers, can lock in a geography for a century.
Roback: Sherwin Rosen in 1979 and Jennifer Roback in 1982 asked what happens when both workers and firms can move. The Island now has six towns. Here are their wages, and their rents. They differ a lot. But if people can move, no town can be better than another, all things counted: a high wage must be offset by a high rent or by a place nobody enjoys, and a lovely place must cost more or pay less. Utility, not income, is equalized.

That turns prices into a measuring instrument. Whatever people pay in rent beyond what the local wage makes up for, they pay for the place itself: its weather, its coast, its schools, its safety. On the Island the amenities are planted, and reading them back from wages and rents recovers them exactly. Lagoon, by the beach, is the nicest; Ridge the least. David Albouy built indices like this for American cities, and Part forty-eight uses the same logic to value clean air.

Now shock the Island. Harbour's firms become ten percent more productive. Its wages rise 6.8 percent, people arrive, its population grows 11 percent, and its rents rise 18 percent. Everyone's utility, everywhere, rises 1.5 percent: the gain spreads across the Island, because people move until it does. Instead make Lagoon ten percent nicer. People move in, rents rise 16 percent, and wages fall 3.8 percent: the newcomers pay for the view twice, in rent and in pay. The lesson of spatial equilibrium: a local boom shows up in rents and in the number of people, not in the welfare of the people who live there, and the owners of local land are its surest beneficiaries.
Housing: The last chapter's shocks raised rents more in some towns than others. The difference is the supply of housing. Suppose demand for a town's houses rises by a fifth. Where builders can respond only slowly, with a supply elasticity of 0.6, prices rise 12.5 percent and the stock only 7.5. Where they can build freely, with an elasticity of three, prices rise 5 percent and the stock 15. The same boom becomes expensive houses in one town and more houses, and more people, in the other.

Albert Saiz measured these elasticities for American cities from satellite maps of where land can be built on. Miami, Los Angeles, San Francisco, New York and Boston are all below one; Houston, Atlanta and Charlotte two to three; Wichita over five. The average metropolitan resident lives where it is 1.75. The low ones are hemmed in by the sea and by steep hills, which leave little flat land to build on, and, Saiz found, by stricter regulation, which itself tends to be adopted where land is already scarce and dear.

Does it show in prices? Here are the twenty metropolitan areas with Case-Shiller house price indices: the rise in house prices from 2000 to 2025 against Saiz's elasticity. Prices roughly quadrupled in Los Angeles, Miami and San Diego, and rose least where building is easy. The correlation is -0.42. Consumer prices rose 1.87 times over the same years, so in real terms the coastal cities' houses doubled. The exceptions teach too: Detroit and Cleveland could build, but demand was weak, so prices barely kept up with inflation. Prices need a demand shock and a tight supply.

What does it cost the whole country when the most productive cities cannot grow? In 2019 Chang-Tai Hsieh and Enrico Moretti estimated that tight housing in New York, San Jose and San Francisco kept workers out of the places where they would be most productive, and lowered America's growth by 36 percent between 1964 and 2009. A striking number, widely quoted. In 2026 Brian Greaney published a comment: he found errors in the code, and in a corrected model the gain from loosening the three cities' rules was about a hundredth of the size reported. On the Island, letting Harbour, the most productive town, build freely brings 19 percent more people and cuts its rents 29 percent, but raises the Island's output by only 0.35 percent. Expensive cities clearly transfer income to those who own land in them; how much national output they cost is an open and contested question.
RentControl: Expensive cities are under pressure to cap rents. San Francisco gave economists a clean test. In 1994 its voters extended rent control to small multi-family buildings built before 1980, while those built later stayed uncontrolled. Rebecca Diamond, Tim McQuade and Franklin Qian compared tenants and landlords in buildings on either side of that line, before and after the law, tracking where tenants moved for years afterwards.

Two findings. Tenants in controlled buildings were about 20 percent less likely to move, and less likely to be displaced from the city: rent control did what it promised for the people it covered, a transfer worth thousands of dollars a year each. But landlords of controlled buildings cut the rental housing they offered by 15 percent, selling to owner-occupiers and redeveloping their buildings. Fewer rental homes push up the rents that everyone else pays, so the law's cost fell on future renters. Rent control is a transfer from landlords and future tenants to current ones, paid for partly in lost housing.
Neighbourhoods: Schelling's board sorts people into neighbourhoods. Does the neighbourhood then change them? Comparing families in rich and poor areas confuses the place with the people who chose it, the sorting problem of chapter four. From 1994 to 1998 an American experiment called Moving to Opportunity enrolled 4,604 families living in public housing in 5 cities, and a lottery split them into three groups: vouchers they could use only in low-poverty neighbourhoods, ordinary housing vouchers, or nothing. Chance, not choice, decided who moved.

Early studies found little effect on the parents' earnings, though their health improved. Then, in 2016, Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren and Lawrence Katz followed the children into adulthood with tax records. Children whose families used the experimental voucher before they turned thirteen earned about 3,477 dollars a year more in their mid-twenties, 31 percent more than the control group's 11,270. They were more likely to go to college, and less likely to become single parents. Children who moved as teenagers gained nothing, and did slightly worse, perhaps from the disruption. The gain grows with the years of childhood spent in the better place. Part forty maps this exposure effect for every county in America.
Berlin: Chapter eleven. The Berlin Wall as an experiment.

Agglomeration is hard to measure because places that are productive attract people, and people make places productive. Berlin offers an experiment no one would design. Before the war it was one city, its business centre in the district of Mitte. In 1961 the Wall cut West Berlin off from that centre, which lay in the East. In 1989 it fell, and the city was joined again. Gabriel Ahlfeldt, Stephen Redding, Daniel Sturm and Nikolaus Wolf collected land values and employment for thousands of city blocks in 1936, 1986 and 2006, and asked what the division and the reunion did to each.

Their model is a city of many blocks in which people choose where to live and where to work, commute between them, and make each other more productive when they work close together. Agora solves a small version: sixty blocks on a line. Joined, most jobs crowd around the old centre, just east of where the Wall will run: 77 percent of them. Now build the Wall. The western half must employ its own people, and a new centre grows in the West, around what had been a secondary district, as the area by the Zoo station did in West Berlin.

And prices. On the line city, division lowers floor prices most in the western blocks next to the Wall, about 29 percent relative to the West's average, and raises them around the new western centre. Reunification runs the film backwards. That is the pattern the authors found in Berlin's land values. Fitting their model to it, they estimated that a block's productivity rises with the employment nearby, with an elasticity of 0.07, and that the effect fades within a few minutes' travel. Residents, too, value nearby residents, with an elasticity of 0.16. Agglomeration is strong, but intensely local: it lives in the blocks around you.
Transport: How much is a railway worth? Dave Donaldson answered for the vast network built in colonial India, using archival records of prices, trade and harvests district by district. Guided by a model of trade between districts, he found four things. Railways cut the cost of trade, and the gaps between prices in different districts shrank. Trade rose, between districts and with the world. Real agricultural income rose about 16 percent in a district once the railway reached it. And the gain was what the trade model's formula predicted from the change in trade shares, the formula of Parts thirty-five and thirty-six. Von Thünen's railway, measured.

Highways reshaped American cities. Between 1950 and 1990 the population of central cities fell 17 percent, while their metropolitan areas grew. Nathaniel Baum-Snow used the interstate plan of 1947, drawn for other reasons, to predict where highways would go, and found that each new highway through a central city cut its population by about 18 percent. Without the interstates, central cities would have grown about 8 percent. It is the car of chapter three. In the Island's town, commuting thirty percent cheaper moves the share of households within eight kilometres of the centre from 69 percent to 49.

The largest move to the cities in history happened in China. In 1980 about 20 percent of Chinese lived in towns and cities; by 2025, about 58 percent, catching up with the world. It happened despite the hukou, a household registration system that ties a family's access to schools, health care and pensions to the place where it is registered. Hundreds of millions of migrants worked in the cities, often leaving their children behind in the village. Moving costs, whether made by distance, by highways or by law, decide how fully people can follow opportunity.
Place: Can policy make a place? The most dramatic case is Shenzhen. In 1980 China made this small city across the border from Hong Kong a special economic zone, with its own rules for foreign firms, land and labour. In 1979 it had about 314 thousand residents; the census of 2020 counted 17.56 million, 56 times as many. But Shenzhen was a door through which a whole country opened to the world, so it is hard to say what the zone itself did, and there is no Shenzhen without China.

America's largest experiment was the Tennessee Valley Authority. From 1933 the federal government built dams, power lines, roads and canals across one of the poorest regions in the country. Patrick Kline and Enrico Moretti compared the region with others that had been proposed for similar authorities but never got them. Gains in farming lasted only as long as the money, and reversed when the transfers wound down. Gains in manufacturing kept growing long after: a big push that, once started, sustained itself through agglomeration. But for the nation the local agglomeration largely moved activity from elsewhere; what raised national productivity, by more than it cost, was the infrastructure itself.

Who gains from a subsidy to a place? The Island answers with spatial equilibrium. Give Harbour, where housing is hard to build, a subsidy worth ten percent of productivity. Its rents rise 18 percent and its population 11; everyone's utility on the Island rises 1.5 percent. Give the same subsidy to Grove, where building is easy: rents rise only 7 percent, the town grows 20 percent, and everyone gains 2.2 percent. Where housing is tight, much of a place-based subsidy ends up as rent for local landowners. Some economists conclude that policy should help people, not places; others answer that where joblessness is concentrated and persistent, as in Part thirty-six's China-shock towns, places are how you reach the people.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: planning, property and transport.

Who does this for a living? City governments employ planners and housing economists who estimate what a zoning rule or a new tower will do to supply and to rents. Property firms employ analysts who price buildings by their features and their place on the rent gradient, and forecast where a city will grow. Transport ministries appraise a new line by the time it saves, and some, as in Britain, add the extra productivity of a denser, better-connected city, using elasticities like this part's dial. And retailers and logistics firms use gravity models to decide where to put a shop or a warehouse.

Called it? In 1997 Frances Cairncross, a journalist at The Economist, published The Death of Distance. As communication became nearly free, she argued, distance would stop deciding its cost, location would matter less to most decisions of business, and more people would work from home. The cost of communicating did collapse, and after 2020 about a quarter of America's paid working days were worked from home, 26 percent over the last year of data. But economic activity kept concentrating in large, expensive cities, and their wage premium grew. The verdict: partly right. Cheaper communication made the places where people meet more valuable, not less.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: remote work and the climate.

The frontier begins with the largest change in how people work in a century. In 2019 about 7 percent of America's paid working days were worked from home. In May 2020, in the pandemic, about 62 percent. And then it did not go back: over the last year of the survey of José María Barrero, Nicholas Bloom and Steven Davis, about 26 percent, nearly four times the old level, and steady. Some people moved from city centres to the suburbs and smaller towns; office buildings lost value. Whether this loosens the hold of the big cities, or only lengthens the commutes of those who still come in two or three days a week, is being measured now.

The frontier's open questions. Remote work: if ideas spread face to face, as Marshall thought, can a city's learning survive when its workers meet less? The climate: many of the world's most valuable places sit on coasts and river mouths; heat, floods and rising seas will reprice them, and someone must decide where to defend and where to retreat. Density and emissions: dense cities use less fuel per person, but they are also richer. Sorting: how much of the big-city premium is the city, and how much is who chooses to live there? And housing: how much output do tight cities cost the nation, a number that moved by two orders of magnitude in one comment.
